questions.question: Explain why scrap metal is valuable, the separate routes ferrous and non-ferrous scrap follow, and the three things recycling saves.
questions.expected_answer: Metal melts down into metal as good as new, so scrap can replace freshly mined metal. Ferrous scrap is baled and sold to a steel mill, where it is melted in an electric arc furnace into reinforcing bar, sheets and cans; non-ferrous scrap goes to separate smelters, copper to be refined into wire, aluminium into cans and frames, brass into taps. Recycling saves ore, since every tonne of scrap steel leaves a tonne of iron ore in the ground; energy, since melting scrap uses far less than smelting ore and recycled aluminium needs only about five percent of the energy of new aluminium; and landfill space. The magnet crane at the dealer's yard makes the two routes possible by separating the metals, and sorted loads fetch a better price.

questions.question: Describe who gleaners are, what they do, and why a technology project should think about them.
questions.expected_answer: Gleaners, also called waste pickers or reclaimers, collect cans, wire, appliances and off-cuts from bins and skips before municipal trucks arrive, sort them and sell them by the kilogram at buy-back centres or scrap dealers; tens of thousands do this in South Africa and they divert a large share of recyclable material from landfill at no cost to the municipality. Their work is honest and skilled: they know which metals pay, use a magnet to tell steel from aluminium and strip copper from old motors; many belong to cooperatives with identity cards. A project should consider people as well as the product, because a crane that sorts faster lets the dealer pay promptly and fairly for mixed loads, which benefits the gleaners who brought them.

questions.question: Explain why metal theft is serious, what the law requires of scrap dealers, and how to tell legitimate scrap from stolen metal.
questions.expected_answer: Thieves cut live copper cables, telephone and railway wire, lift cast-iron manhole covers and take brass and bronze fittings because the metal sells; a cable worth a few hundred rand as scrap can black out a suburb for days, stop trains and cost thousands to replace, and people have died in open manholes and on live cables. Dealers must be registered, record every seller's name, identity number and address, hold metal for a period before selling it on and refuse infrastructure metal; buying stolen metal is itself a crime and some metals need permits. Legitimate scrap was thrown away or given by its owner, like a bin can or a demolition gutter; cable with burnt-off insulation, manhole covers and railway fittings have no honest source and the burn marks are the clue.
